name: Polybius
title: The Cursed Arcade Game That Never Existed
claims: Polybius is an urban legend about a mysterious arcade video game that appeared in Portland, Oregon in 1981 | [1]
The gameplay of Polybius was supposedly psychoactive, abstract, and dangerous, causing amnesia, seizures, night terrors, and hallucinations | [1]
Players were said to be so addicted they returned until they went insane, died, or vanished | [1]
The lack of surviving cabinets is explained by men in black who recorded data and removed the machines | [1]
There is no evidence for any Polybius machines in the 1980s | [1]
The earliest known print reference is the September 2003 issue of GamePro | [1]
The earliest online reference to Polybius is a coinop.org page dated to 1998 | [1]
There is no record of the publisher Sinneslöschen, and no surviving cabinet has ever surfaced | [1]
People claiming to have seen Polybius may be conflating memories with unusual actual titles like Cube Quest and Tempest | [1]
In 1981, two Portland residents became ill while playing games at the same arcade | [1]
Ten days after the illness, the FBI raided multiple Portland arcades for illegally converting games into gambling machines | [1]
Parents expressed concern that video game arcades could be dangerous, and there were reported cases of epileptic seizures | [1]
A teenager died while playing Berzerk, leading to rumors of a cursed arcade game | [1]
Urban legends spread of arcade cabinets built to hypnotize players, influencing science fiction like Robert Maxxe's novel Arcade | [1]
Atari covertly tested unfinished games in real arcades to monitor player reactions | [1]
The urban legend has had a lasting cultural impact in journalism, music, television, film, and performance art | [1]
Two video games titled Polybius were released in 2007 and 2017 claiming a connection to the purported arcade | [1]
Fact-checking website Snopes calls the game a modern-day version of 1980s rumors about men in black recording high-score initials | [1]
No ROM image of the arcade machine's software has ever surfaced | [1]
The coinop.org page was first uploaded a few years after 1998, indicating the upload date was fabricated | [1]
Archives of the coinop entry from 2000 contain the text 'New addition - anyone heard of this game?' | [1]
The GamePro feature story 'Secrets and Lies' declared the game's existence to be 'inconclusive' | [1]
The GamePro author only heard about the legend when the owner of coinop.org contacted him | [1]
Inverse concluded the game was almost certainly invented to promote coinop.org | [1]
Brian Dunning describes Sinneslöschen as not-quite-idiomatic German meaning 'sense delete' or 'sensory deprivation' | [1]
Sinnlöschen would be a more standard German construction | [1]
Polybius shares its name with the classical Greek historian Polybius, born in Arcadia, known for verifying through eyewitnesses and the Polybius square | [1]
The game was supposedly housed in a simple black cabinet | [1]
Players supposedly suffered from seizures, amnesia, insomnia, night terrors, and hallucinations | [1]
Children formed lines around the cabinet and fought for access | [1]
It is claimed machines were visited by men in black who collected unknown data but left coins inside | [1]
It was said the game could turn itself on autonomously | [1]
Some accounts connected Polybius to the CIA's MKUltra mind control program | [1]
Michael Lopez developed a migraine headache after playing Tempest and was found unconscious in a stranger's yard | [1]
During a filmed Asteroids world record attempt at the same arcade, another teen played for 28 hours until suffering stomach pain | [1]
The FBI made 52 Portland arcade arrests in 1981 and 25 arrests at a single arcade north of Portland a year later | [1]
A 1980 New York Times article commented on potential for video game addiction | [1]
The National Safety Council claimed video games promoted violence | [1]
There are nine recorded cases of arcade games triggering epileptic seizures in the 1980s | [1]
In 1982, a teenager died while playing Berzerk in Calumet City, Illinois, due to heart failure not triggered by the game | [1]
Rumors in the late 1970s and early 1980s circulated of arcade machines designed to hypnotize, brainwash, or recruit players | [1]
These rumors influenced The Last Starfighter and Robert Maxxe's novel Arcade | [1]
Atari employees swapped in test versions of unfinished games and observed player responses without disclosing the true nature to patrons | [1]
The US military commissioned Atari to modify Battlezone into a tank training simulator called The Bradley Trainer in the early 1980s | [1]
Newspapers covered The Bradley Trainer and programmer Ed Rotberg in 1981 | [1]
In the late 1990s, Doom II was modified into a virtual training program for marines called Marine Doom | [1]
Cube Quest used laserdisc technology to create hallucinogenic environments and resulted in frequent breakdowns and early removal | [1]
Poly-Play was the only arcade video game developed in East Germany and had a similar name and typeface | [1]
Judd Ruggill proposed Tempest as an influence because it is abstract, geometric, and inspired by the creator's nightmares | [1]
No archived Usenet posts discuss Polybius, but the Publius Enigma was discussed on Usenet in the early 1990s | [1]
Polybius appeared as a central cameo in the Nine Inch Nails music video 'Less Than' | [1]
Polybius had cameos in The Goldbergs, The Simpsons, and Loki | [1]
A Polybius cameo in Paper Girls gave the series 1980s science fiction credentials | [1]
Artists Goto80 and Raquel Meyers explored the theme in performances in 2010 | [1]
The Polybius Conspiracy is a seven-part podcast published in 2017 adapted from a canceled feature film | [1]
A novel by Collin Armstrong was published in 2025 through Gallery | [1]
In 2007, Rogue Synapse published a free downloadable game titled Polybius for Windows at sinnesloschen.com | [1]
Dr. Estil Vance founded a corporation bearing the name Sinnesloschen | [1]
In 2016, Llamasoft announced Polybius for PlayStation 4 with PS VR support | [1]
Jeff Minter initially claimed to have played the original in Basingstoke, England, but later admitted it was a contribution to the hoax | [1]
Minter's game is closer to his work on Tempest successors Tempest 2000 and TxK | [1]
Ben Silverman of Yahoo! Games remarked there is no evidence the game ever existed | [1]
Ripley's Believe It or Not! called Polybius the most dangerous video game to never exist | [1]
Joe Streckert called Polybius the video game equivalent of H.P. Lovecraft's Necronomicon | [1]
Portland Monthly calls it one of Portland's craziest urban legends and mentions speculation about MKUltra | [1]
Coinop.org page includes a purported screenshot of the title screen allegedly from a ROM image file | [1]
A coinop.org update on May 16, 2009, promised further information after a trip to Kyiv, Ukraine | [2]
